rows.text: 2009 charcoal Beta 266127 came from tepetate over Rock 3 in C:East (1730 ± 40 BP, 230–410 CE 2sigma), whereas Beta 266128 came from behind the C:North stacked rock wall (1760 ± 40 BP, 140–390 CE 2sigma); neither directly fixes the calendar year the wall was built.

Two 2009 charcoal tests in deep C:West fill near Blockage 12 are Beta 266129 in Layer 5d (1810 ± 40 BP, 120–260 and 280–330 CE 2sigma) and Beta 266130 in Layer 5h (1700 ± 40 BP, 240–420 CE 2sigma). These later-than-expected dates admit several depositional explanations; attribution to cave termination remains Sload's interpretation.
Burial 6 stone-walled chamber 5.0 x 4.5 m, 2 m high; 9.6 m north of composite Building 5 center and 4.6 m south of main-platform center; tentative Building 5 assignment about AD 300
Burial 6 contained 12 individuals, 6A–B complete centrally and 6C–L lacking skulls and first cervical vertebrae in northern area; bound arms suggested by their position

Burial 6 central 18 obsidian eccentrics formed nine pairs of undulating knives and feathered serpents; above were pyrite disk and anthropomorphic figurines; provisional faunal counts at least 2 canines, 4 felines, 14 birds
Burial 5 individual 5C wore composite shell-greenstone ear ornaments and shell disk necklace; decayed wooden object beside right arm, hands covering puma mandible

Torras Freixa distinguishes earth-and-stone fills of Moon Pyramid Buildings 1–3, earth-dominant Building 4, earth/tepetate Sun Pyramid fill, and stone/mud compartment-cell construction of the Feathered Serpent Pyramid, associated with contrasting talud and talud-tablero façades.

Torras Freixa reports Murakami's assumptions: one worker per five-person household, five hours per day procurement and transport, eight hours manufacture and assembly, 30/60/100 construction days per year, yielding conditional estimates of under ten years per pyramid; notes 50-year discrepancy in Early Tlamimilolpa placement relative to Rattray chronology.

Sload documents more than 20 pieces of slate at the cave's eastern terminus, with only two likely slate pieces in a C:West Layer 5f rodent burrow outside that concentration; terminal specimens include pyrite-bearing slate and cleaved pieces with drilled holes, some interpreted cautiously as possible mirror backs or pendants. Magnetite from the B:West BYCT layer and gypsum from B:East excavation backdirt were also illustrated.

The TE28 Area D fire pit associated with charcoal determination Beta-220763 yielded a flower-pot censer rim and body fragment weighing 68.1 g. Sload illustrates a white post-firing wash and red fugitive pigment identified in the caption as cinnabar. The object may represent ritual use before emplacement of the overlying concrete floor; that activity sequence remains the excavator's interpretation.

One surviving Feathered Serpent tenoned head on the west facade retains two obsidian disk eye inlays. Barnes's photograph documents this head only; it does not establish the total number of heads once inlaid.

Author photographs and discussion document obsidian insets in Quetzalpapalotl patio-carved columns in three motifs: mythological bird eyes, separate eye disks, and profile mirror-bowl patterns in bird tails. Not all empty sockets prove original obsidian inlays.

In 2002, Carballo excavated 1.253 m³ of Deposit 1 within a shallow depression in tepetate, retrieving 170.6 kg of screened obsidian debitage (136.16 kg/m³). The feature reached 42 cm below surface and was estimated to be one-third of the surviving truncated deposit.

Table 3.1 assigns 534 small pottery fragments from Deposit 1: Miccaotli 168, Tlamimilolpa 173, Xolalpan 157, Tzacualli 27, Patlachique 3, Coyotlatelco 7, Aztec 1. Excavators used paste-based identification for heavily eroded sherds; the Xolalpan association is contextual, not a radiocarbon date.

In the analyzed subsets Carballo counted 31,690 lithics (18.86 kg) in Deposit 1, 5,542 (3.51 kg) in Deposit 2, and 2,859 (7.86 kg) in Deposit 3. Average artifact masses were 0.60, 0.63 and 2.75 g respectively; the larger fragments in Deposit 3 reflect a different reduction regime.

In Table 5.1 Deposit 3 is visually classified as 45% gray, 53% green and 2% mahogany obsidian, including 22% of the total provisionally attributable to Tulancingo. Carballo explicitly contrasts the 22% visual figure with roughly 50% Tulancingo in a nonrandom geochemical subset, rejecting the subset as representative of the deposit.

Carballo compares four methods for extrapolating dart-point production from Deposit 1's lithic waste. The modeled estimates span 1,836–11,760 points, with a mean of 4,358; removing the model with a 3.4% assumed preform-breakage rate yields mean 3,242. These are modeled possible output quantities, not directly observed projectile counts.
